title: Designing Heuristics
html:
A* is only as good as its heuristic. Good heuristics are admissible, as close to the true cost as possible, and cheap to compute — and the standard way to invent one is to relax the problem.

Two classic 8-puzzle heuristics

HeuristicDefinitionRelaxed problem it solves exactly
h₁ — misplaced tilesNumber of tiles not in their goal squareA tile can jump anywhere in one move
h₂ — Manhattan distanceSum over tiles of |row − goal row| + |col − goal col|A tile can move to any adjacent square, even an occupied one

A relaxed problem has more actions, so its optimal cost can only be lower — that is why a heuristic derived from a relaxation is automatically admissible (and consistent).

All three find the optimal 26-move solution; Manhattan distance does it with roughly 40× fewer expansions than no heuristic.

Dominance and the effective branching factor

Dominance — if h₂(n) ≥ h₁(n) for every n and both are admissible, h₂ dominates h₁ and A* with h₂ never expands more nodes. Larger is better — as long as it stays admissible.

To compare heuristics independently of problem size, compute the effective branching factor b*: the branching factor a uniform tree of depth d would need to contain the N nodes A* expanded. Close to 1 is ideal.

N + 1 = 1 + b* + (b*)² + … + (b*)ᵈ

Recipes for heuristics

Relax the problem

Remove constraints until the problem is easy to solve exactly: straight-line distance (ignore roads), Manhattan distance (ignore other tiles), ignore-preconditions in planning.

Max of admissible heuristics

h(n) = max(h₁(n), …, hₖ(n)) is admissible and dominates each component — use it when no single one is best everywhere.

Pattern databases

Precompute exact costs for a sub-problem (e.g. tiles 1–4 only) for every configuration and look them up. Disjoint patterns can be added. Solves the 15-puzzle and Rubik's cube quickly.

Learn a heuristic

Train a model to predict cost-to-go from features of a state (AlphaGo's value network is a learned evaluation). Fast, but no admissibility guarantee.

DomainAdmissible heuristic
Grid, 4-way movesManhattan distance |dx| + |dy|
Grid, 8-way moves (diagonal cost √2)Octile distance max(dx, dy) + (√2 − 1)·min(dx, dy)
Any-angle / road mapsEuclidean (straight-line) distance
Travelling salespersonCost of a minimum spanning tree of unvisited cities
Watch out

Manhattan distance is not admissible on an 8-connected grid — one diagonal step (cost √2 ≈ 1.41) covers Manhattan distance 2, so it overestimates.

What makes a heuristic admissible? Give one for the 8-puzzle.

It never overestimates the true cost to the goal. Manhattan distance: every tile must move at least its row and column offset, one square per move, so the sum can't exceed the real number of moves.

Admissible vs consistent?

Admissible: h(n) ≤ h*(n). Consistent: h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′) for every edge — a stronger condition that implies admissibility and guarantees f is non-decreasing along paths, so graph-search A* never needs to re-open nodes.

If h₂ dominates h₁, is h₂ always better?

It never expands more nodes, but it may cost more to compute per node. The best heuristic balances accuracy against evaluation time.
